title: Henry Red Allen's band, the Metropole and 'Feeling Good'
summary: He joins the Metropole crowd and Red Allen for eight years and tells how he came to help on the 'Feeling Good' record.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: And when I came back to New York I met the people that owned the Metropole. That was in '54. And then, after that, I joined...I played...they had a place on Eighth Avenue, over near Madison Square Garden and I played over there for a while,
then finally I went and joined Henry Red Allen and I stayed with Red eight years. Until he died, you know.

But I quit again, out at the Blue Spruce Inn. That's when we made the record "Feeling Good." Now let me tell you about that record. Red and I...I say, "Red, I'm getting sick and tired of you again, so I gotta go." He said, "'Bye." So I went on. Well, that was on a Saturday night, but on Sunday we were off, you know. And Monday he had this recording engagement for John Hammond, "Feeling Good." And I knew that he would get Lannie Scott. And I knew that Lannie didn't know... because if I'd been playing with him eight years I'd know... you know, even when I'd go out later, Lannie would go in as substitute. But Lannie could not play those things that Red wanted played, and I knew it.

So this Monday night I went out...I got in my car and I said, "Well, I might as well go help this turkey out." So I got in the car, drove all the way out to Hollis. When I walked in, John Hammond and...what's this other guy's name, was...

Not Frank D'riggs...could have been...But anyway, I walked in. When I walked in, Red Allen said to John Hammond, "Here's this politician now." And I said, "Well, Red, come on, man, I came out to make you sound good." So we made it "Feeling Good," "Cherry", and all the other things. And that was the last time I played with...

One other time he asked me to do a television show with him...a morning talk show. And I did this talk show with him. But other than that...and then a strange thing...a few months later he called me and says, "You know what," he says, "You're losing one of your best friends." I didn't know what the hell he was talking about. But he had cancer. And I said, "Well, so what." You know. I always, you know, turned him off like that. "So what. So I'm losing one of my best friends. If you're talking about yourself, you're not my best friend." Although we were...you know...he was my best friend and I considered myself his best friend.

Shortly after he died I decided that I'd had it in music. So then I got out again. In 1954...when did he die? He died in '67. Yeah, '67, yeah. Well, in 1954, I went...I'd made a record for Jazztone with Jonah Jones and...
Pete Brown and Vic Dickenson and...who was the drummer? Cole.
